claim: Opinion-citation overlap is a valid recall measure for legal research

evidence.quote: LegalCiteBench evaluates exact recovery relative to an opinion-anchored authority set rather than exhaustive legal research over all potentially relevant authorities
these reference sets should not be interpreted as the only legally relevant authorities for open-ended research questions
Relevance assessments based on citations are not appropriate. This is because a decision may cite another decision for any number of reasons, for any number of different topics.
actually selecting relevant documents that simply have not been cited (false negatives)

note: Overlap measures recall of what one court cited, not of responsive authority; 2605.10186 says so in its own scope statement. Precision and MAR computed against the same list also count real uncited authorities as errors.

claim: Published independent studies measure AI time savings in patent prosecution

evidence.quote: In the 10-day drafting task, treated participants finished an estimated 10 minutes faster than controls (p = 0.05), against a control-group mean of 110 minutes.
Funding for the direct costs of this experiment was provided by Google.
I found no disclosed or peer-reviewed study of time savings for office-action response drafting, a core part of prosecution.

note: Narrowly confirmed for drafting only: one pre-registered RCT (Autor et al. 2026, working paper, not peer reviewed) measured about 9% (10/110 min), p = 0.05 at 10 days and p = 0.27 at 90 days. It is Google-funded with six Google authors, so it is not independent of AI-industry interests, and it covers benchmark drafting, not office actions or prior-art search. No study measures prosecution proper (office-action responses), hence unresolved.

claim: Published independent studies measure AI allowance-rate gains

evidence.quote: No. I found no independent study, whether pre/post, difference-in-differences, or RCT, linking AI drafting or prosecution tools to allowance-rate changes.
Nor is there a general obligation to disclose to the USPTO the use of such tools
Autor et al. (2026) measure rubric quality only, with no USPTO outcomes, so the study cannot speak to allowance.

note: A finding of absence within this session's search. The only allowance-lift figures are vendor self-comparisons (DeepIP, Rowan, Juristat). A structural reason is that 89 FR 25609 imposes no AI-use disclosure, so USPTO data carry no AI flag.

claim: The 2605.10186 out-of-reference audit omits its sample size, sampling frame, category rates and inter-rater agreement

evidence.quote: For a sampled subset of Cat1 and Cat2 model outputs, reviewers inspect concrete citations or case authorities that were produced by the model but not matched to the opinion-derived reference set.
This audit is not used to replace the main opinion-anchored scoring protocol.

The section text gives no number of audited out-of-reference authorities, no counts or rates for categories (i)–(iv), and no description of how the "sampled subset" was drawn (which models, how random).
A search of the full HTML text for "kappa", "inter-annotator", "inter-rater", "agreement" and "Cohen" found none in a validation context.

note: The only reported validation table (100 root cases, 3 reviewers, about 2,100 examples, 90.5% pass) covers construction fidelity, not completeness. The code or data release was not checked.

claim: 2605.10186 scores a real but uncited authority the same as a fabricated one

evidence.quote: The output JSON contains matched citations, fabricated or unmatched citations, missed ground-truth citations, the number of predicted citations, and the number of ground-truth citations.
Precision penalizes fabricated citations, recall penalizes missed citations, and F1 is scaled to 0–100.
We do not treat τ as a universal legal correctness boundary, but as a benchmark-specific low-overlap criterion.

note: MAR above 94% is therefore a low-overlap rate, an upper bound on fabrication rather than a fabrication rate. F1 is a lower bound on legal usefulness.

claim: No legal benchmark reports a measured miss rate for opinion-citation ground truth

evidence.quote: No published, measured rate of "unmatched but responsive" authorities for any common-law citation benchmark was found.
I found no study that re-judges COLIEE, AILA, ECtHR-PCR or any US case-law citation benchmark with lawyers to measure the share of uncited-but-responsive authorities.

note: A finding of absence within this session's search, reported independently by two research lanes, not a proof. ECtHR-PCR hypothesises false negatives without measuring them, and 2605.10186 defines category (iv) but reports no rate.

claim: In the nearest measured analogue (1804.07583), most system citations scored as false positives against the existing citation were judged acceptable

evidence.quote: in many cases our suggestion was equal to (38.2%) or even preferred (19.4%) over the ground-truth suggestion.
The inter-rater agreement between workers was 64%.

note: 11,803 re-judged false positives from Wikipedia news-citation recommendation, crowd-judged; precision rose by an average of 18%. Not legal authority, and the share is of system errors, not of the corpus.

claim: LeCaRD/LeCaRDv2 is the only public legal case-retrieval dataset found with pooled, multi-annotator expert relevance judgments and reported agreement

evidence.quote: a two-level candidate set pooling strategy
Each annotation task is completed repeatedly by three different annotators... The Kappa value for the Overall Relevance is 0.5190.
This is the only case-retrieval benchmark found in this pass that uses TREC-style pooling with expert relevance judgments.

note: Chinese criminal law, where courts do not cite. US attorney-judged collections exist but are small (AIRS, few queries, unreliable for unpooled methods) or internal (Turtle/Westlaw). Absence of others is within this session's search.

claim: Common-law case-retrieval benchmarks derive relevance labels from the citations a court actually made

evidence.quote: These datasets define relevance criteria as the precedents cited in the query document, utilizing citation as a signal to construct the dataset.
The relevant passage of a query is defined as the passage its central citation cites to.
In COLIEE, the cases cited are considered relevant.

note: Also LePaRD, AILA 2019, CaseHOLD, AusLaw citation prediction and SG-LegalCite. Expert checks in these datasets cover construction quality, not completeness.

claim: Expert-graded legal research evaluations (Magesh et al., VLAIR) do not compute recall of responsive authority

evidence.quote: we find a Cohen's kappa of 0.77 and an inter-rater agreement of 85.4%
For some questions, there could be an almost limitless number of potential sources.

Our evaluators were allowed to exercise discretion where they felt the reference answer had minor errors or was less complete than ideal, so that correct and more complete responses would not be penalized.

note: Magesh grades correctness and groundedness; retrieval misses are discussed only qualitatively. VLAIR publishes no rate of more-complete-than-reference credits and no evaluator agreement.

claim: Expert relevance labels in legal retrieval are themselves noisy

evidence.quote: We find that 64% of the documents judged relevant in 2006 were again judged relevant in 2007
No set of appeals had a success rate lower than 0.7 and ten had a success rate greater than 0.9.
The Kappa value for the Overall Relevance is 0.5190.

note: 10-18% of previously non-relevant documents flipped to relevant on re-judging. A single expert pass is not truth; adjudication and multiple assessors are needed.

claim: TREC Legal's pooled, Topic-Authority-adjudicated protocol estimates recall over the collection rather than against a reference list

evidence.quote: The sets of documents submitted by the participants in a topic allow for a straightforward submission-based stratification of the document collection.
The Topic Authority then renders a final judgment on all appealed assessments.
which reflect sampling error but not assessment error

note: E-discovery responsiveness, not case-law research. In 2009, 5 of 24 runs reached estimated recall of 0.7 or more.

claim: LLM relevance judges reach kappa of about 0.67 against expert labels on LeCaRD

evidence.quote: the human-annotated golden labels in LeCaRD
all experiments are conducted in Chinese, due to substantial differences between Chinese and foreign legal systems.

note: GPT-3.5 0.67 (legal facts) / 0.62 (material facts); fine-tuned Qwen-2 0.69 / 0.60; Llama-2 0.41 / 0.25 (the research note's transcription of table values, not author prose). Chinese only; there is no English common-law validation against attorney labels.

claim: Vendor time and allowance figures for AI patent tools lack study design

evidence.quote: Every vendor figure found is self-reported. None comes with a study design, comparison group, sample size, or workload definition.
Cut prosecution time in half and boost your allowance rates.
One client saved approximately 555 attorney hours in a single quarter.
Customers report up to 60–80% time savings on drafting while maintaining or improving quality

note: DeepIP's own figures disagree (40%, 50%, 70%). Rowan's "18% reduction in the number of Office Actions" and Juristat's +14.5 points are also uncontrolled customer self-comparisons.

claim: In the patent-drafting RCT, the quality gain is larger and more robust than the time saving

evidence.quote: AI access raised the quality of work delivered on benchmark patent drafting tasks at 10 days (0.34 SD, p = 0.03) and 90 days (0.38 SD, p = 0.01), with larger gains among junior lawyers.
The 90-day estimate is similar in size, at 10 minutes, but less precise (p = 0.27).
AI access did not reduce redlining time for either group.

note: Google-funded working paper; 133 randomized, 91 completed (32% attrition); tasks capped at two hours, which compresses time differences.

claim: The Schwarcz et al. legal-AI RCT contains no patent tasks

evidence.quote: 127 law students from the University of Minnesota and the University of Michigan law schools.
A full-text grep for "patent" in the paper returned 0 hits.

note: Its 34-140% productivity gains come from six non-patent tasks with law students, so they do not transfer to prosecution.

claim: Lawyers' perceived recall in Blair & Maron (at least 75%) far exceeded measured recall (about 20%)

evidence.quote: The study found that while users thought they had retrieved at least 75% of relevant documents, they had retrieved close to 20%.

note: Low confidence: secondhand via Locke & Zuccon's survey; the primary CACM paper (DOI 10.1145/3166.3197) was not read. This is a discovery setting, not case law.

claim: Different legal research databases return largely non-overlapping relevant results (Mart 2017)

evidence.quote: An average of 40 percent of the cases were unique to one database, and only about 7 percent of the cases were returned in search results in all six databases

note: Secondhand only: secondary sources disagree on some figures and the paper's tables were not verified. Consistent with incomplete single lists, but not usable as a primary number.
